questions.question: Explain how both the rescue device project and the cell phone tower project followed the design process, naming the investigation and design activities in each.
questions.expected_answer: Both followed IDMEC as a loop. Term 1 investigation: the crash scenario, levers and mechanical advantage, and the syringe tests of pneumatics and hydraulics; Term 1 design: a brief with specifications and constraints, fitness-for-purpose considerations, sketches, an oblique and a working drawing of the rescue device; then making the syringe-and-card model, testing against each specification and presenting it. Term 2 investigation: examining a cell phone tower and its cousins, analysing a desk and a radio, comparing landline and mobile systems, and the stiffening and triangulation tests; Term 2 design: a tower brief with specifications, two oblique sketches, group evaluation and improvement, a resource list and a one-face working drawing; making, evaluating and communicating follow.

questions.question: A learner says a tube is stronger than a flat sheet and a stable tower cannot bend. Correct both statements and define the three terms involved.
questions.expected_answer: The tube is not stronger; the material and its breaking load are unchanged. The tube is stiffer, because rolling moves material away from the line of bending so it resists bending far more. A stable tower can still bend: stability is the ability to stay upright without toppling, which depends on the base, the centre of gravity and anchoring, while rigidity is the ability to resist bending or changing shape. Strength is the ability to carry a load without breaking. A tower must be stable, strong and rigid, and these are three different properties.

questions.question: Compare first, second and third class levers, and explain how a hydraulic system and a lever both give a mechanical advantage while obeying the same trade-off.
questions.expected_answer: First class has the pivot between effort and load, reverses direction and can have MA greater than, equal to or less than 1 depending on the pivot position. Second class has the load between pivot and effort, keeps direction and always has MA above 1. Third class has the effort between pivot and load, keeps direction and always has MA below 1 but moves the load further and faster. A hydraulic system multiplies force because the same pressure acts on a larger piston area, in proportion to the areas; a lever multiplies force in proportion to the ratio of effort arm to load arm. In both, the gain in force is paid for by a proportional loss in distance moved, because no machine gives out more work than is put in.
